newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK -- Supply, election key.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK -- Supply, election key.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury market will shift its focus from economic news to a slew of new supply and the elections in the coming week, which could put pressure on bond prices, players said.
Treasuries soared this past week, boosted by economic data that indicated the economy is growing at a moderate clip, but with no signs of intensifying inflation.
"After the deluge this week, numbers take a back seat to the outcome of the elections and the Treasury auctions," said Stuart Hoffman, chief economist at PNC Bank Corp.
"After the big runnup, we might be do for a period of resting," he added.

Outside of the weekly indicators -- jobless claims, chain store sales and mortgage financing -- the lone monthly report scheduled for release is construction spending, which is not typically a big market mover.

Therefore, the Treasury's quarterly refunding takes center stage. After the selling $28.0 billion of T-bills on Monday, the Treasury will auction $18.5 billion of three-year notes on Tuesday, $10 billion 10-year notes on Wednesday and $10 billion of 30-year bonds on Thursday.
Market participants, for the most part, don't forsee any problems taking down the new supply.

"Supply is never a problem when you have a bullish sentiment," said Joseph Carson, chief fixed income economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, adding that the concerns the market had months ago are virtually gone. "Given the friendly (economic) data, a firm dollar and lower commodities prices, there won't be much of a concession needed" for successful auctions.
Still, some concession is inevitable, said Neil DeSarno, head trader at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp.
"The Street is long, so in order to make room for supply, the market will probably go down a bit," he said. "The market needs to get a little concession to do supply successfully."
However, DeSarno said it would not surprise him if the market stayed put, because, "the bulls are still very much in control."

Players were confident the market can add to the past week's gains, possibly bringing bond yields down to about 6.50 percent -- a level not seen since early March. The bond was last closed below 6.50 percent March 7, when it was 6.46 percent.
But it's unlikely that the bond will breach below that level, because there's too much resistance there, said Deutsche's Carson.
On the flip side, CIBC's DeSarno said he did not think the bond will move above 6.70 percent in the near term.
"We're going to get a Fed that will stay on hold, perhaps through all of 1997, so in that scenario, bond yields can do a lot better," he said. "For now, the market should hold here."
Market participants also said that periphiral markets, including the dollar and commodities, will be closely monitored.
The dollar's rise to nearly 115 yen this week helped boost bonds, as did the falling commodities prices.
Late Friday, the bond was at 100-29/32, down 14/32 from Thursday. Its yield rose to 6.68 percent from 6.64 percent.
Federal Funds are expected to open at 5-1/4 percent to 5-3/8 percent.

Meanwhile, the election is on many people's minds, but predicting market reaction has proven difficult. Most players agreed that a victory by President Clinton, but the Republicans keeping control of Congress would be a non-event for the market.
But should the Democrats regain control of the House of Representatives, that could pose a problem, because, traders said, Democrats spend more and that could boost the budget deficit.
But after positive readings on manufacturing, employment and wages the last few sessions, market participants said the market's wounded psyche may be healed.
"Right now," says PNC's Hoffman, "there's no question we have a positive undertone to the market."
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1660
